children.text: An 18th-century Baroque church in the center of Hagonoy, Bulacan, declared a National Shrine of Saint Anne in 1991. It is the heart of devotion to St. Anne, known locally as Apo Ana, and hosts the Palaisdaan Festival around her July 26 feast day.
The National Shrine of Saint Anne in Hagonoy stands in Barangay Santo Niño in the town proper of Hagonoy, Bulacan, about
54km

northwest of Manila. Its official name is the National Shrine and Parish of Saint Anne, and it belongs to the Diocese of Malolos. Locals fondly call St. Anne Apo Ana; "apo" is a respectful Tagalog word meaning grandparent or ancestor. As the mother of the Virgin Mary and the maternal grandmother of Jesus, St. Anne is regarded as a patron of the elderly, parents and grandparents.

Hagonoy is a low-lying town north of Manila Bay, tangled with rivers and fishponds, and is known for raising prawns and milkfish, earning it the title of aquaculture capital of Bulacan. In such a place the church has long been the center of town life. According to Wikipedia and other sources, Hagonoy began around 1581 as a visita (chapel-of-ease) of Calumpit and was entrusted to the Augustinian friars. Sources give the founding year as 1580, 1581 or 1591, so it is safest to think of it as the late 16th century.

The present building dates from the 18th century. A stone and brick church built in 1731–1734 burned down in August 1748, and the present church is said to have been begun in 1747 on its current site, moved to avoid flooding, and completed in 1752. It later survived a fire in 1856 and earthquake damage in 1871, and was extensively renovated in 1936, 1961 and 1968–1970. As a result, the exterior is an older Baroque frame overlaid with mid-20th-century work. It was declared a National Shrine on October 29, 1991.

It is not as flashy as famous tourist sights, but it is a good place to see how Philippine Catholic faith continues in everyday town life. It pairs well with other church visits in Manila or Bulacan as a half-day addition, and around the July feast you can even see a boat procession on the river, so timing your visit makes it much richer. The word "National" in its name means the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) recognizes it as a pilgrimage site of nationwide importance. Even if you are not Catholic, you can take in 18th-century church architecture and local devotional culture at once, which suits anyone curious about everyday faith in a Philippine provincial town. One hour is enough for a quick visit, and half a day for a relaxed one.

The facade has three arched entrances with carved hardwood doors, and images of Augustinian saints stand atop its pilasters. The central pediment holds a rose window and a scene of St. Anne with the young Mary, with a cross held by two angels at the top. What you see today was heavily reworked in the 1968–1970 renovation. Daylight brings out the texture of the stone, so late morning gives the clearest photos.

The rectangular bell tower on the left of the church originally had five levels, and a sixth level and a dome were reportedly added in the latest reconstruction. Its decoration is restrained, with semicircular arched windows and corner buttresses. For a balanced photo, take it from the plaza together with the whole church. The bells often ring at Mass times, so timing your visit adds to the atmosphere.

blocks.title: Apo Ana image on the main altar

children.text: The main altar enshrines a carved wooden image of St. Anne. She is shown teaching Scripture to the young Mary, and devotees dress her with clothes, crowns and flowers donated over the years. The garments and decorations change from time to time, so each visit looks a little different. Note also the composition of the young Mary seated with a book beside her; the image of a grandmother teaching the faith is at the heart of this devotion.

A perpetual novena to St. Anne is said to be prayed on Tuesdays. Weekdays are fairly quiet, but more local worshippers may come to pray on Tuesdays. The shrine says pilgrims may gain an indulgence, so Catholic visitors may want to check the shrine's official pages.

July is called the month of Apo Ana, with events building up to her feast on the 26th. Tied to the town's founding anniversary, the month-long Palaisdaan Festival is held, with a boat procession (pagoda) moving along the river before a procession continues to the church. In 2023, about 300 motorized boats were reported to have taken part.

blocks.title: Last Sunday of April thanksgiving festival

children.text: This is known as a town festival of thanksgiving for deliverance from past calamities, in which the patron saints of the barangays join the procession and the traditional dance called Lerion is performed. The date and program can change from year to year, so it is best to check the shrine's announcements.

Mass and a procession in honor of St. Anne mark the day the church was declared a National Shrine. 2026 is the 35th anniversary. It tends to be less crowded than July, making it an option for those who want to see the shrine quietly.

The area around the church is a low-lying town of fishponds, waterways and landings. Shrimp paste (bagoong alamang) and processed meat are said to be the main products, so a walk through the market lanes for local food after visiting the church fits well. Since the area floods often, lanes further in can be muddy in the rainy season, so bring light footwear.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: Half a day from Manila to the shrine

children.text: Leave Manila. By private car or ride-hailing it takes around
1 hour 30 minutes
, and by bus it may take longer. Allow extra time for weekday morning traffic.
Arrive in Hagonoy town and first photograph the triple arches and bell tower from the plaza in front of the church.
Step inside and slowly look at St. Anne on the main altar, the ceiling and the side altars. If a Mass is in progress, sit quietly at the back.
Look around the souvenir and candle sellers near the church, and if you wish, light a candle or pray to St. Anne.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town. Being an aquaculture town, fish and shrimp dishes are good choices.
Walk through the town market and the landing area to browse local products such as shrimp paste, then head home.
Combine it with Malolos Cathedral or Barasoain Church for a one-day Bulacan church tour. The trip from Hagonoy to Malolos is said to be by jeepney.
During feast week there may be traffic restrictions, so arrive early and decide where to park or be dropped off.
Take in the Mass and novena atmosphere at the church, and look around the street decorations and festival preparations.
Check the boat procession schedule along the river. Dates and routes may change from year to year.
Watch the faithful's procession on the plaza around the time it reaches the church.

The 2023 procession was reported to have been held on Saturday, July 22, so it may fall on a different date from the feast day itself on the 26th. Be sure to check that year's announcement from the Hagonoy local government (LGU).
According to Wikipedia, Baliwag Transit and First North Luzon Transit serve Hagonoy, with routes from Divisoria, Monumento, Cubao and Pasay. Intervals are described as about
30 minutes
to
45 minutes
Routes and schedules can change, so confirm at the terminal before departing.
From the town center, it is a short tricycle ride to the church.

items.title: By private car or ride-hailing from Manila

children.text: A route from Manila via NLEX and MacArthur Highway is described, with a distance of about
54km
and a travel time of about
1 hour 30 minutes
With ride-hailing it may be hard to find a car back, so it is safer to arrange a round-trip hire or have the driver wait.
Tricycles are said to be the most common mode of transport in Hagonoy.
Jeepneys run toward Malolos and Paombong.

For a quiet, reverent visit, the dry season from November to May is more comfortable. Hagonoy is low-lying and often floods in the rainy season; annual rainfall is about 792mm, heaviest from June to September. In August 2026 as well, parts of the town were reportedly underwater for more than two weeks after typhoons and monsoon rains, so check the latest news in the rainy season.
July is the time to see the festival, but weigh the weather and flooding risk. The thanksgiving festival on the last Sunday of April and the October 29 anniversary are also options.

Hagonoy is close enough for a day trip, so many visitors stay in Manila or Malolos. There may be small guesthouses in town, but confirm details locally.

For food, being an aquaculture town, milkfish, shrimp dishes and grilled fish are recommended. Wikipedia lists shrimp paste (bagoong alamang) as a main processed product, so looking for a small pack as a souvenir is one option. No restaurant names are given here because there is no reliable information.

Planning meals and rest in Manila or Malolos before and after the visit makes the schedule more solid. In Hagonoy town you may find small restaurants and local cafes, but opening hours can be irregular, so we suggest stopping by with time to spare around lunchtime. Bring enough cash, and break large bills into small change.
The church is a place of worship, so wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees.
During Mass, avoid flash and loud noises, and check first whether photos toward the altar are allowed.
The Mass schedule is said to be available on the shrine's official website and Facebook page.
During July feast week, arrive early and check road closures and parking.
In the rainy season, bring sandals or boots and an umbrella, and check flood news in advance.
Keep small change ready for buses and tricycles.
Combine Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church to make a Bulacan church circuit.
Keep your belongings in front of you and watch for pickpockets at crowded events.
The shrine's website links to official accounts such as Facebook and Instagram, which are good places to check event announcements.
Prices of candles and religious items from stalls near the church vary widely, so ask the price before buying.
Hagonoy is low-lying and suffers prolonged flooding in the rainy and typhoon seasons. Check the latest weather and road news before you leave.
Worship comes first inside the church, so refrain from walking around and taking photos during Mass.
Founding and construction dates differ between sources, so use the signage and the shrine's announcements as your reference.
Festival dates and boat procession routes can change from year to year, so check the town hall's announcements.
Public transport routes and schedules can change, so reconfirm locally.
The cathedral of Malolos, the provincial capital of Bulacan, is said to be reached by jeepney. It pairs well with Hagonoy.
A historic church in Malolos associated with the constitution of the First Philippine Republic.
The church of Calumpit, to which Hagonoy is said to have belonged early on as a visita. Confirm travel time locally.
